title: Black holes
part: IV: Orbits, stars, and black holes
one_line_summary: Takes the Schwarzschild geometry all the way down to r = 2M and below: shows that the light cones narrow and then tip over so that inside the horizon decreasing r is the future, introduces the tortoise coordinate to tame the logarithms in coordinate time, contrasts the finite proper time of a plunging astronaut with the diverging coordinate time and logarithmically delayed signals seen from afar, computes her tidal stretching and her view of the sky, and ends with stellar collapse drawn on spacetime and Penrose diagrams.
role_in_book: Chapters 21-24 built the Schwarzschild metric and studied radial plunges, orbits and photon paths outside a star. Chapter 25 is the first chapter that treats the metric as describing empty space all the way in, so the awkward radius r = 2M can no longer be hidden inside matter. It stays deliberately within Schwarzschild coordinates, collecting every symptom of trouble at the horizon (closing light cones, infinite coordinate time, infinite redshift) together with the evidence that nothing local goes wrong there (finite proper time, smooth tidal components). This sets up Chapter 26, which classifies singularities and removes the horizon pathology with Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates, and Chapter 27, which completes the picture with Kruskal-Szekeres coordinates and a fuller Penrose diagram. The Penrose diagrams here reuse the conformal machinery of Chapter 19, and the observational examples anticipate gravitational waves in Chapter 46.

assumed_background.topic: The Schwarzschild line element, its static and asymptotically flat character, and Birkhoff's theorem
Radial plunge from rest at infinity: proper time tau(r) and coordinate time t(r)
Conserved energy from the time-translation symmetry (p_t constant) and gravitational redshift for static observers, eqn 22.16
Critical emission angle for photons in the Schwarzschild geometry and the photon orbit at r = 3M
Orthonormal frames (vielbeins) of static observers and measured energy E = -p.u
Geodesic deviation in an orthonormal frame and the Schwarzschild Riemann components
Penrose diagrams, conformal infinity (i+, i0, scri) and spacelike Big-Bang singularities
Light cones and the classification of intervals as timelike, null or spacelike
Geometrized units G = c = 1 with M standing for GM/c^2
Integrating rational functions to logarithms and substitutions such as u = r^(1/2)
Newtonian escape speed and the idea of tidal stretching
Basic stellar evolution: main sequence, red giant, white dwarf, neutron star; binary-star mass estimates

learning_objectives: Reader can derive the radial light-cone slope dt/dr = +/-(1 - 2M/r)^-1 from ds^2 = 0 and use it to sketch how cones narrow as r approaches 2M from outside.
Reader can substitute r = 2M - epsilon into the Schwarzschild metric and show that, inside the horizon, a displacement in r at fixed t is timelike, so r plays the role of time and t that of space.
Reader can explain why every future-directed worldline inside r = 2M must reach r = 0, and why this makes r = 2M an event horizon.
Reader can define the tortoise coordinate, integrate it to r* = r + 2M ln|r/2M - 1| + const, and write the radial metric in the conformally flat form (1 - 2M/r)(-dt^2 + dr*^2).
Reader can state what the tortoise coordinate fixes (45-degree radial light rays, no metric blow-up) and what it does not (the horizon sits at r* = -infinity).
Reader can contrast the finite proper time of a radial plunge with the divergent Schwarzschild coordinate time, and read both behaviours off Figs. 25.5 and 25.6.
Reader can use the orthonormal-frame Riemann components to show that tidal accelerations are finite at r = 2M, stretch radially and squeeze transversely, and diverge as r goes to 0.
Reader can compute the coordinate travel time of an outgoing radial photon, eqn 25.15, and explain from its logarithm why a distant observer sees an infalling source slow down, fade and never cross.
Reader can use the critical angle sin(psi_c) = sqrt(27) M (1 - 2M/r)^(1/2)/r to find the fraction of sky a black hole blocks for a static observer, including the half-sky result at r = 3M.
Reader can derive the blueshift factor (1 - 2M/r)^(-1/2) of starlight measured by a static observer from conservation of p_t and the vielbein.

Reader can describe the collapse of a sufficiently massive star through r = 2M, explain why outside observers never see the singularity, and interpret the Penrose diagrams of a collapse black hole, including why r = 0 is a spacelike singularity.
Reader can summarize the four main lines of observational evidence for black holes and quote the scale r_S of about 3 km per solar mass.

teaching_approach.summary: An informal, symptom-by-symptom investigation that refuses to leave Schwarzschild coordinates. Every section poses a physical question (what happens to light cones at r = 2M, what does a falling astronaut feel, what do we see of her, what does she see, how does a real star get there) and answers with a short calculation from the metric plus a picture. The recurring tension is between quantities that blow up in these coordinates and quantities that stay finite for the traveller, and the chapter deliberately leaves that tension partly unresolved so that the better coordinates of the next two chapters arrive as a relief. Humour (Achilles, Brad Pitt, 'bon voyage'), boxed examples and margin notes carry the history and the observational context.
narrative_arc: Define a black hole, restate Schwarzschild via Birkhoff, and point to the two suspicious radii r = 0 and r = 2M, noting that for real black holes the region below 2M is empty space rather than stellar interior.
Promise that r = 2M is a coordinate artefact (finite proper time, smooth curvature) and pause for the observational case for black holes (Sgr A*, X-ray binaries, quasars, gravitational waves).
Outside the horizon: derive the radial light-cone slope and watch the cones close up as r approaches 2M, linking this to the infinite coordinate time of the plunge from Chapter 22.
Inside the horizon: substitute r = 2M - epsilon, discover that fixed-t displacements in r are timelike, and conclude that the future points to r = 0; name the event horizon.
Assemble a full light-cone picture in Schwarzschild coordinates and flag its apparently singular null curves as illusory, deferring the cure.

Declare that studying black holes is largely a search for good coordinates, introduce the tortoise coordinate to package the recurring logarithms, illustrate it with Zeno's race, and show it straightens radial light rays while pushing the horizon to r* = -infinity.

Death of an astronaut: compare proper time and coordinate time for the plunge, compute her tidal stretching from the Riemann tensor, and confirm that nothing special happens locally at r_S while r = 0 is a genuine physical singularity.
Signals from the astronaut: integrate the outgoing null condition to get a logarithmically divergent delay, so distant observers see pulses spread out, redden and dim.
Looking around: use the photon critical angle and time-reversal symmetry to show the hole swallowing more and more of the sky, and use conserved p_t to show incoming starlight is blueshifted.

Gravitational collapse: stellar endpoints and the Chandrasekhar limit, a collapsing star crossing r = 2M with its light cones, the frozen appearance from outside, and Penrose diagrams showing a spacelike singularity hidden behind the horizon.
Exercises build Painleve-Gullstrand ('rain') coordinates, which are regular at r = 2M, as a preview of Chapter 26.
signature_moves: Diagnose the causal character of a coordinate by freezing all the others and checking the sign of ds^2, turning the slogan 'the future is inwards' into a two-line calculation.

Draw the same physical process twice against two different clocks (proper time and Schwarzschild time, Figs. 25.5 and 25.6) so that the coordinate nature of the horizon divergence is visible at a glance.
Let the traveller's body be the curvature detector: tidal accelerations from orthonormal Riemann components are smooth at r_S and blow up only at r = 0.
Name a coordinate after a paradox (Achilles and the tortoise) so that its defining asymptotic behaviour, approaching but never reaching, sticks.
Tell the story from both viewpoints: what the falling astronaut experiences, what the distant observer receives, and what the astronaut herself sees.

Cash in a result prepared earlier: the critical photon angle and its time-reversed reading were set up in §24.2 with an explicit promise, and here they become the astronaut's view of the sky, followed by a new blueshift calculation.

Deliberately leave the horizon pathology unresolved within the chapter, flagging it as illusory, so that the next chapter's coordinate change has a clear motivation; the end-of-chapter exercises then quietly provide one fix.
Use margin notes for coordinate-philosophy cautions ('a variable called t has no special claim to be time') at exactly the moment the metric makes that point.

sections.title: Chapter opening: what a black hole is and the two awkward radii
sections.summary: Defines a black hole as a region from which light cannot get out and argues via Birkhoff's theorem that a non-rotating one is described by the Schwarzschild metric. Points out that the line element misbehaves at r = 0 and at r = 2M: at the latter g_tt vanishes (static clocks would record no time, signals are infinitely redshifted) and g_rr diverges. Restoring units, r_S is about 3 km per solar mass, which for ordinary stars lies deep inside the matter, but for a black hole all the mass sits at the centre and the region below 2M is vacuum. The chapter then asserts that local physics and curvature are smooth at r_S, that a traveller crosses it in finite proper time, and that the trouble stems from the coordinates.
key_moves: Invoke spherical symmetry plus Birkhoff to justify using the Schwarzschild metric for the whole exterior of a non-rotating hole.
Identify two separate failures at r = 2M: vanishing g_tt (clock rate and redshift) and diverging g_rr (proper radial distance per dr).
Put in numbers: r_S = 2GM/c^2 is about 3 km for one solar mass.
Observe that for a black hole the region 0 < r < 2M lies outside the mass, so the horizon can no longer be ignored.
Anticipate the resolution: finite proper time to cross, smooth curvature, so the divergence is a coordinate artefact to be removed later.

sections.title: Example 25.1: observational evidence for black holes
sections.summary: A boxed survey of indirect evidence in four families: stellar proper motions around Sagittarius A*, whose shadow and bright ring were imaged by the Event Horizon Telescope; X-ray binaries in which an unseen companion is too heavy to be a neutron star, with Cygnus X-1 as the standard case; compact, massive, highly luminous engines at galactic centres such as quasars; and gravitational-wave signals from merging black holes. A margin note dispels the idea that black holes vacuum up their surroundings: outside the horizon the geometry is that of any spherical star.
key_moves: Stellar orbits near the Galactic Centre require a compact mass of about 4 million solar masses.
In a binary, the visible star's motion fixes the companion's mass; above neutron-star limits it must be a black hole; accreted gas heated by its orbital motion shines in X-rays.
Galactic nuclei and quasars need enormous energy output from a small volume, explained by accretion onto supermassive holes.
Gravitational-wave detections of mergers are flagged for Chapter 46.

sections.title: The surface r = 2M
sections.summary: Outside r = 2M, setting ds^2 = 0 for radial motion gives light-cone slopes dt/dr = +/-(1 - 2M/r)^-1, which are 45 degrees far away and become vertical as r approaches 2M from above, so cones close up and any worldline takes ever more coordinate time to change r. Inside, writing r = 2M - epsilon shows that a displacement purely in epsilon at fixed t is timelike while t has become spacelike. Hence the light cones tip over, the future of every event points to smaller r, even light is trapped, and nothing inside can be seen from outside: r = 2M is the event horizon. A full light-cone map in Schwarzschild coordinates (Fig. 25.3) shows null curves racing to infinite t at r_S, a feature the authors label as illusory.
concepts: radial light cones in Schwarzschild coordinates
closing of light cones near the horizon
exchange of timelike and spacelike roles of t and r inside the horizon
inevitability of reaching r = 0 inside the horizon
coordinates have no intrinsic metric meaning
key_moves: Set ds^2 = 0 with dtheta = dphi = 0 to get dt/dr = +/-(1 - 2M/r)^-1.
Read off asymptotic slope +/-1 at large r and slope diverging as r approaches 2M from above: cones become needle-thin in the (r, t) plane.
Link narrowing cones to the infinite coordinate time for a plunge found in Chapter 22.
Substitute r = 2M - epsilon to get ds^2 = epsilon/(2M - epsilon) dt^2 - (2M - epsilon)/epsilon depsilon^2 + (2M - epsilon)^2 dOmega^2.
Freeze t, theta, phi: ds^2 < 0, so epsilon is a time coordinate that must keep increasing, driving r to 0; t is spacelike.
Apply to a photon emitted inside: both edges of its cone head to smaller r, so it and every massive particle are trapped.
Name r = 2M the event horizon by analogy with the Earth's horizon.

sections.title: The tortoise coordinate
sections.summary: Because coordinate-time integrals of the form int dr/(1 - 2M/r) keep producing logarithms, the authors define r* by dr*/dr = (1 - 2M/r)^-1, giving r* = r + 2M ln|r/2M - 1| + const, which runs to minus infinity at the horizon. Example 25.2 motivates the name with Zeno's race: as r* is decreased without limit, r creeps toward 2M but never reaches it. Radial null curves become t = +/- r* + const and the radial metric takes the form (1 - 2M/r)(-dt^2 + dr*^2), so cones no longer close and nothing blows up at r = 2M. The price is that the horizon has been pushed off to r* = -infinity, so better coordinates are still needed.
concepts: logarithmic divergence of coordinate time at the horizon
conformally flat form of the radial Schwarzschild metric
radial null geodesics in Schwarzschild spacetime
key_moves: Spot the recurring integral Delta t = int dr/(1 - 2M/r) and its logarithm.
Define dr*/dr = (1 - 2M/r)^-1 and integrate to r* = r + 2M ln|r/2M - 1| + const.
Tell the Achilles race: dr/dr* goes to zero near 2M, so r approaches 2M only as r* goes to minus infinity.
Write light rays as t = +/- r* + const.
Factor the radial metric as (1 - 2M/r)(-dt^2 + dr*^2): radial cones are at 45 degrees in (r*, t).
Note the remaining drawback: the horizon is at infinite r*, motivating Chapter 26.

sections.title: Death of an astronaut
sections.summary: An astronaut plunges radially, flashing a torch at regular intervals. Her proper time as a function of r is a smooth power law, so she reaches r_S and then r = 0 in finite time with nothing special on her watch; the Schwarzschild coordinate time, which is the proper time of distant observers, diverges logarithmically at r_S. Example 25.3 reuses the orthonormal-frame tidal equations: radial stretching at rate 2M/r^3 and transverse squeezing at M/r^3, finite at the horizon but unbounded as r goes to 0, which marks r = 0 as a true physical singularity. Integrating the outgoing radial null condition gives the photon delay (r2 - r1) + r_S ln[(r2 - r_S)/(r1 - r_S)], so distant watchers see her pulses arrive ever further apart and increasingly redshifted, and she never quite appears to reach the horizon.
concepts: proper time versus coordinate time at the horizon
Riemann tensor in the static orthonormal frame
radial null geodesics in Schwarzschild spacetime
apparent freezing and redshifting of infalling sources
key_moves: Quote tau(r) for a plunge from rest at infinity: finite and smooth through r_S (Fig. 25.5).
Quote t(r) with its logarithmic term: divergent at r_S (Fig. 25.6).
Evaluate the deviation equation with Schwarzschild orthonormal Riemann components to get d^2chi/dtau^2 = +2M/r^3 chi radially and -M/r^3 chi transversely.
Note the components depend only on M/r^3, so nothing singular happens at 2M but they diverge at r = 0.
Integrate dt/dr = (1 - r_S/r)^-1 from emission to reception to find the flat-space delay plus a logarithm that diverges as emission approaches r_S.
Translate into observations: pulses spread out, the image appears to hover near the horizon, and light is increasingly redshifted (quantitative falling-observer redshift deferred to Chapter 26).

sections.title: Looking around near a black hole
sections.summary: Reuses the critical photon angle from Chapter 24: light emitted at radius r beyond psi_c spirals in, and psi_c shrinks to zero at the horizon. Since the metric is symmetric under time reversal, the same angle limits which incoming rays reach an observer at r; the remaining directions are dark, and that dark patch is the black hole as seen. Example 25.4 finds that at r = 3M the hole fills half the sky, and a margin note adds that there one can see the back of one's own head. Close to the horizon the outside universe shrinks to a small bright cone, and incoming starlight measured by a static observer is blueshifted by (1 - 2M/r)^(-1/2), obtained from conserved p_t and the static vielbein.
concepts: time-reversal invariance of the Schwarzschild metric
apparent angular size of a black hole
measured energy from the orthonormal frame
key_moves: Recall sin psi_c = sqrt(27) M (1 - 2M/r)^(1/2)/r and note psi_c goes to 0 at r = 2M.
Invoke time-reversal symmetry to convert an escape criterion for emitted photons into an acceptance criterion for received photons.
Evaluate at r = 3M: psi_c = pi/2, so the hole covers half the sky.
Compute E_obs as the hatted time component of p using (e_t)^t-hat = (1 - 2M/r)^(1/2).
Use p_t = (1 - 2M/r)p^t constant to get p^t(r) = hbar omega_inf (1 - 2M/r)^-1, hence E_obs = hbar omega_inf (1 - 2M/r)^(-1/2).

sections.title: Gravitational collapse
sections.summary: Sketches stellar endpoints: ordinary stars end as white dwarfs, but above the Chandrasekhar limit (about 1.4 solar masses) collapse continues to a neutron star or, for still larger mass, through r = 2M to a central singularity. Figures 25.8 and 25.9 show the stellar surface worldline with light cones tipping as it crosses the horizon. From outside the star seems to slow, redden and freeze just above r_S; light emitted exactly at r_S hovers there, and light emitted later falls in whichever way it is aimed, forming a closed trapped surface. The Penrose diagrams (Figs. 25.10 and 25.11) place the horizon H at 45 degrees and draw r = 0 as a spacelike line, explained by the swapped roles of r and t inside; anyone who crosses H meets it, while observers reaching i+ see everything except the interior.
concepts: apparent freezing and redshifting of infalling sources
Penrose diagram of a collapse black hole
key_moves: Chain the stellar endpoints: white dwarf below about 1.4 solar masses, neutron star above, black hole for the heaviest remnants.
Follow the stellar surface through r = 2M in an (r, t) sketch and a 3D sketch with light cones.
Reuse the delayed-pulse result: the image freezes and blackens as the surface nears r_S from outside.
Classify light emitted at and after horizon crossing: outgoing front stays at 2M, everything later is dragged inward.
Draw the Penrose diagram with horizon H and a double-line singularity, and argue the singularity is spacelike because r is timelike inside.

Read visibility off the Penrose diagram: observers ending at i+ see everything except r < 2M, while anyone inside meets the singularity along 45-degree light rays and has a future horizon cutting off light from most of space.
Add the stellar interior (hatched fluid) to the diagram, showing its surface crossing H and ending on the singularity.

sections.title: Chapter summary and exercises
sections.summary: The summary restates the four headline points: Schwarzschild describes non-rotating holes, r_S is the horizon beyond which r = 0 is unavoidable, crossing r_S is locally unremarkable while the tidal field grows without bound toward r = 0, and proper time to the singularity is finite though coordinate time diverges. The four exercises construct Painleve-Gullstrand ('global rain') coordinates by a coordinate change and by a physical array of dropped clocks, use the rain metric to show inward motion inside the horizon, and analyse whether a tangentially launched particle can avoid capture.
key_moves: Coordinate change dt = dT - R(r) dr chosen so that g_rr = 1 yields a metric regular at r = 2M with flat constant-T slices.
Operational construction of rain time from clocks dropped from rest at infinity at a steady rate.
Use the rain metric's null directions to show inward motion inside the horizon.
Relate a local tangential speed to conserved E and L to test capture.

concepts.name: black hole
concepts.definition: A region of spacetime bounded by an event horizon, from inside which no signal, not even light, can reach distant observers; the non-rotating, uncharged vacuum case is described by the Schwarzschild geometry.
concepts.how_introduced: Opens the chapter as a working definition, tied to Birkhoff's theorem, with a margin history from Michell and Laplace's escape-speed 'dark stars' to Oppenheimer-Snyder and Wheeler's name.
concepts.notes: The Newtonian dark-star idea gets the radius 2GM/c^2 right by coincidence; light in Newtonian gravity could still rise and fall back, whereas in GR nothing inside the horizon even moves outward.

concepts.name: Schwarzschild metric
concepts.definition: The unique spherically symmetric vacuum solution of Einstein's equation, ds^2 = -(1 - 2M/r)dt^2 + (1 - 2M/r)^-1 dr^2 + r^2 dOmega^2, describing the exterior of any spherical mass and the whole of an uncharged non-rotating black hole.
concepts.how_introduced: Restated at the start as the geometry that Birkhoff's theorem forces on a spherical black hole; then examined near and inside r = 2M in its own coordinates.

concepts.name: Birkhoff's theorem
concepts.definition: Any spherically symmetric vacuum region of spacetime is a piece of the Schwarzschild geometry, whatever the (spherical) matter inside is doing, so it is static and fixed by the single parameter M.
concepts.how_introduced: Cited in one sentence to justify using Schwarzschild for a non-rotating black hole; also underlies the margin remark that the exterior of a hole is no different from that of a star of the same mass.

concepts.name: Schwarzschild radius
concepts.definition: The radius r_S = 2GM/c^2 (2M in geometrized units) at which g_tt of the Schwarzschild metric vanishes and g_rr diverges; for a black hole it is the location of the event horizon.
concepts.how_introduced: Singled out as one of two radii where the line element misbehaves; numbers are restored to show it is about 3 km per solar mass, inside ordinary stars but in empty space for a black hole.

concepts.name: coordinate singularity
concepts.definition: A place where metric components blow up or vanish only because of a poor choice of coordinates; invariant quantities such as curvature and the proper time of travellers remain finite there, and a coordinate change removes it.
concepts.how_introduced: Built up by accumulation: curvature is smooth at 2M, a plunging clock crosses in finite proper time, tidal forces are unremarkable, yet coordinate time and light-cone slopes diverge. The chapter names the conclusion but saves the systematic treatment for Chapter 26.
prerequisites: proper time versus coordinate time at the horizon
Riemann tensor in the static orthonormal frame

concepts.name: curvature singularity
concepts.definition: A boundary of spacetime at which curvature, and hence tidal accelerations felt by any object, grow without bound, so that no coordinate change can make it regular; for Schwarzschild it is r = 0.
concepts.how_introduced: Contrasted with r = 2M: the tidal equations of Example 25.3 scale as M/r^3 and diverge only as r goes to 0, so any body reaching r = 0 is destroyed.
prerequisites: Riemann tensor in the static orthonormal frame
concepts.notes: The book gives component values rather than an invariant; the Kretschmann scalar 48M^2/r^6 (not in this chapter) is the cleaner proof.

concepts.name: event horizon
concepts.definition: The boundary of the region of spacetime from which no future-directed causal curve can reach distant (future null) infinity; for Schwarzschild it is the null surface r = 2M.
concepts.how_introduced: Named after showing that light cones inside r = 2M tip over so that even outward-aimed photons move to smaller r; compared with the Earth's horizon beyond which we cannot see; later drawn as a 45-degree line H on Penrose diagrams.
prerequisites: exchange of timelike and spacelike roles of t and r inside the horizon
inevitability of reaching r = 0 inside the horizon
concepts.notes: Only the local, coordinate-based argument is given here; the global definition via future null infinity is implicit in the Penrose-diagram discussion.

concepts.name: radial light cones in Schwarzschild coordinates
concepts.definition: For radial motion ds^2 = 0 gives dt/dr = +/-(1 - 2M/r)^-1, so in an (r, t) plot the light cones have 45-degree edges far away, become arbitrarily thin as r approaches 2M from above, and are tipped over for r < 2M.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived in one line from the metric and illustrated with a row of cones (Fig. 25.2) and a map of null curves (Fig. 25.3).

concepts.name: closing of light cones near the horizon
concepts.definition: In Schwarzschild coordinates the coordinate speed of light dr/dt = +/-(1 - 2M/r) goes to zero at r = 2M, so cones pinch to vertical lines and any causal worldline needs unbounded coordinate time to change r.
concepts.how_introduced: Read off eqn 25.3 as r decreases toward 2M and tied to the infinite coordinate time of the Chapter 22 plunge.
prerequisites: radial light cones in Schwarzschild coordinates
concepts.notes: A coordinate effect: in coordinates regular at the horizon the cones do not pinch.

concepts.name: light cone
concepts.definition: The set of null directions (ds^2 = 0) at an event, dividing tangent directions into timelike (inside), null (on) and spacelike (outside); massive particles move inside it.
concepts.how_introduced: Assumed from special relativity and used as the main diagnostic tool of the chapter.

concepts.name: exchange of timelike and spacelike roles of t and r inside the horizon
concepts.definition: For r < 2M the metric coefficient of dr^2 is negative and that of dt^2 positive, so a displacement along r is timelike and along t spacelike; the Schwarzschild r then behaves as a time coordinate that must decrease into the future.
concepts.how_introduced: Found by substituting r = 2M - epsilon, freezing t, theta and phi, and noticing that the remaining interval is negative; a margin note stresses that a coordinate labelled t has no special claim on time.
prerequisites: coordinates have no intrinsic metric meaning
concepts.notes: Whether r must decrease rather than increase is a choice of time orientation (black hole versus white hole); the chapter assumes the black-hole branch.

concepts.name: inevitability of reaching r = 0 inside the horizon
concepts.definition: Inside a Schwarzschild horizon every future-directed timelike or null worldline has decreasing r and ends at r = 0 within a finite affine parameter or proper time, regardless of the rocket thrust applied.
concepts.how_introduced: Follows from the tipped-over cones: an astronaut inside who fires a photon in any direction still sends it inward.
prerequisites: exchange of timelike and spacelike roles of t and r inside the horizon

concepts.name: coordinates have no intrinsic metric meaning
concepts.definition: Coordinates are arbitrary labels of events; physical durations and lengths come only from the metric, so a coordinate named t need not be a time and a coordinate range need not be finite physically.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated in margin notes at the moment t turns spacelike inside the horizon, and again when r* is described as a strange race timer.

concepts.name: tortoise coordinate
concepts.definition: The radial coordinate r* defined by dr*/dr = (1 - 2M/r)^-1, so r* = r + 2M ln|r/2M - 1| + const; it matches r far away and tends to minus infinity as r approaches 2M from outside.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by the logarithms that appear whenever coordinate time is integrated along radial light rays, named after Zeno's paradox (Example 25.2), then used to straighten radial null lines.
prerequisites: radial light cones in Schwarzschild coordinates
logarithmic divergence of coordinate time at the horizon
concepts.notes: The alias Regge-Wheeler coordinate is standard elsewhere, not used in GA. The same formula applies for r < 2M through the absolute value, but that branch is not discussed.

concepts.name: logarithmic divergence of coordinate time at the horizon
aliases: infinite coordinate time to reach r_S
concepts.definition: Integrals of dr/(1 - 2M/r) contain 2M ln|r - 2M|, so the Schwarzschild time for any radial approach to r = 2M, by light or matter, grows without bound even though the approach is finite in proper time.
concepts.how_introduced: Pointed out as the common thread behind the plunge result, the photon travel time and the need for r*.
prerequisites: closing of light cones near the horizon

concepts.name: conformally flat form of the radial Schwarzschild metric
concepts.definition: In coordinates (t, r*) the Schwarzschild metric reads (1 - 2M/r)(-dt^2 + dr*^2) + r^2 dOmega^2, so the radial two-dimensional part is a positive multiple of flat 1+1 Minkowski space and radial light rays are 45-degree lines.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by substituting dr = (1 - 2M/r) dr* into the metric after noting light rays are t = +/- r* + const.
concepts.notes: Conformal factor still vanishes at r = 2M; the horizon has moved to r* = -infinity rather than becoming regular.

concepts.name: radial null geodesics in Schwarzschild spacetime
concepts.definition: Radial light rays satisfy t = +/- r* + const; the outgoing ray from r1 to r2 (both above r_S) takes coordinate time (r2 - r1) + r_S ln[(r2 - r_S)/(r1 - r_S)].
concepts.how_introduced: First as the light-cone edges of §25.1, then written with r*, then integrated explicitly for the astronaut's torch pulses.
prerequisites: radial light cones in Schwarzschild coordinates

concepts.name: radial plunge
aliases: radial infall from rest at infinity
concepts.definition: Free radial fall of a massive particle released from rest at infinity (E-tilde = 1), for which dr/dtau = -(2M/r)^(1/2), giving tau(r) proportional to r^(3/2) and a Schwarzschild time t(r) with a logarithmic divergence at r = 2M.
concepts.how_introduced: Imported from Chapter 22 as the astronaut's trajectory and the backbone of §25.3; also rederived in Exercise 25.2 as the motion of the rain clocks.
concepts.notes: Eqn 25.10 is printed with a plus sign; the minus sign here matches eqn 22.33 and Fig. 25.5.

concepts.name: proper time versus coordinate time at the horizon
aliases: finite proper time, infinite coordinate time
concepts.definition: A radially plunging observer's proper time to reach r_S and then r = 0 is finite (4M/3 from horizon to singularity for fall from rest at infinity), while the Schwarzschild time, which equals the proper time of static observers far away, diverges as she approaches r_S.
concepts.how_introduced: Shown with two side-by-side plots of the same fall (Figs. 25.5 and 25.6) and restated in the chapter summary.
prerequisites: logarithmic divergence of coordinate time at the horizon
concepts.notes: The 4M/3 figure is our own evaluation of eqn 22.33 between r = 2M and 0, not stated in the chapter.

concepts.name: tidal stretching and compression
aliases: tidal forces near a black hole
concepts.definition: Relative acceleration of neighbouring freely falling particles caused by spacetime curvature: near a Schwarzschild mass, separations along the radial direction grow at rate 2M/r^3 and transverse ones shrink at M/r^3, so extended bodies are stretched radially and squeezed sideways.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 25.3 asks what the astronaut feels and reuses the orthonormal-frame deviation equations from Chapter 11; the verdict is nothing special at r_S and fatal, unbounded stretching approaching r = 0.
prerequisites: Riemann tensor in the static orthonormal frame
concepts.notes: The formula uses static-frame components; for a radial boost these particular components are unchanged, which is why they apply to the falling astronaut, a point the book does not spell out.

concepts.name: geodesic deviation
concepts.definition: The separation vector chi between nearby geodesics obeys d^2 chi^i/dtau^2 = -R^i_{tau j tau} chi^j in an orthonormal frame, so the Riemann tensor directly sets relative (tidal) accelerations.
concepts.how_introduced: Quoted in a margin note as the engine behind Example 25.3.
prerequisites: Riemann tensor in the static orthonormal frame

concepts.name: Riemann tensor in the static orthonormal frame
concepts.definition: In the orthonormal frame of Schwarzschild the non-zero curvature components are proportional to M/r^3, with magnitudes 2M/r^3 for the (tau r) and (theta phi) planes and M/r^3 for the mixed planes; none is singular at r = 2M.
concepts.how_introduced: Listed in a margin note to back the claims that curvature is smooth at the horizon and that tidal accelerations follow the pattern of eqn 25.12.
formulas: R_{\hat\tau\hat r\hat\tau\hat r}=-\frac{2M}{r^3},\ R_{\hat\theta\hat\phi\hat\theta\hat\phi}=\frac{2M}{r^3},\ R_{\hat\tau\hat\theta\hat\tau\hat\theta}=\frac{M}{r^3},\ R_{\hat r\hat\theta\hat r\hat\theta}=-\frac{M}{r^3}

concepts.name: apparent freezing and redshifting of infalling sources
concepts.definition: A distant observer receiving light from an object falling toward r_S sees successive signals arrive at ever-longer coordinate intervals and ever more redshifted and dimmed, so the object appears to hover and fade just outside the horizon, although it actually crosses in finite proper time.
concepts.how_introduced: Drawn from the logarithm in the photon travel-time formula for the astronaut's torch, then applied to the surface of a collapsing star, whose image slows, darkens and freezes.
prerequisites: radial null geodesics in Schwarzschild spacetime
proper time versus coordinate time at the horizon
concepts.notes: Quantitative redshift for a falling emitter (exponential in time with scale 4M) is deferred to Chapter 26.

concepts.name: critical angle for photon capture
concepts.definition: For a static observer at radius r, the angle psi_c from the radial direction with sin psi_c = sqrt(27) M (1 - 2M/r)^(1/2)/r separates light rays that escape to infinity from those that spiral into the hole; at r = 2M it is zero, at r = 3M it is 90 degrees.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from Chapter 24 to ask what the astronaut sees; reinterpreted via time reversal as the boundary of the patch of sky from which light can arrive.
prerequisites: time-reversal invariance of the Schwarzschild metric
concepts.notes: The formula defines an angle from the radial line in the static frame; which of psi_c or pi - psi_c bounds the escape cone depends on whether r is above or below 3M, a point the chapter leaves implicit.

concepts.name: photon sphere
concepts.definition: The radius r = 3M at which light can circle a Schwarzschild hole on an unstable orbit; tangential photons emitted there return to their source.
concepts.how_introduced: Appears through Example 25.4 (sin psi_c = 1 at r = 3M) and a margin note that an astronaut there could see the back of her head.

concepts.name: time-reversal invariance of the Schwarzschild metric
concepts.definition: The Schwarzschild metric is unchanged under t to -t, so any null geodesic traversed backwards is also a null geodesic; paths of photons leaving a point mirror those arriving there.
concepts.how_introduced: Carried over from GA §24.2, where the same symmetry was used to turn photon capture into dark patches of sky; here it is applied to the astronaut in one sentence to convert the escape criterion into a visibility criterion.

concepts.name: apparent angular size of a black hole
concepts.definition: The part of an observer's sky from which no light arrives because the corresponding past-directed rays end on the horizon; for a static observer it covers half the sky at r = 3M and nearly all of it as r approaches 2M.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 25.4 evaluates the critical angle at r = 3M and extrapolates toward the horizon, where the outside universe is squeezed into a small cone.
concepts.notes: Valid for a static (hovering) observer; aberration makes a freely falling observer's view different.

concepts.name: conserved Killing energy
concepts.definition: Because the Schwarzschild metric does not depend on t, the covariant component p_t of a geodesic's momentum is constant; for light p_t = -(1 - 2M/r)p^t equals minus the energy measured at infinity.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled in a margin note to find p^t(r) for starlight falling in, and used in Exercise 25.4 through E-tilde and L-tilde.
concepts.notes: Sign conventions are loose in the margin note (p_t written without its minus sign).

concepts.name: measured energy from the orthonormal frame
concepts.definition: The energy an observer measures is the time component of the momentum in that observer's orthonormal frame, equivalently -p.u_obs; for a static Schwarzschild observer this multiplies p^t by (1 - 2M/r)^(1/2).
concepts.how_introduced: Invoked with a margin note that the vielbein method and the dot-product rule of Chapter 22 are the same thing.
formulas: E_{\rm obs}=p^{\hat t}=(\boldsymbol e_t)^{\hat t}p^t,\quad (\boldsymbol e_t)^{\hat t}=\left(1-\frac{2M}{r}\right)^{1/2}

concepts.name: gravitational blueshift of infalling light
aliases: blueshift of starlight near a black hole
concepts.definition: Light falling from infinity toward a mass gains energy as measured by static observers, by the factor (1 - 2M/r)^(-1/2), which diverges at the horizon; it is the gravitational redshift formula read in reverse.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived in two lines for the astronaut looking out, ending with the image of a last tiny patch of blue light.
prerequisites: measured energy from the orthonormal frame
concepts.notes: Applies to static observers; an infalling astronaut's Doppler shift partially cancels it.

concepts.name: gravitational collapse
aliases: stellar collapse to a black hole
concepts.definition: The unhalted contraction of a stellar core whose mass exceeds the limits supportable by degeneracy pressure; its surface passes through r = 2M, forming a horizon, and the matter continues to r = 0.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by asking how black holes are made; told as a stellar-evolution story, then drawn on an (r, t) diagram, a 3D sketch and Penrose diagrams.
prerequisites: radial light cones in Schwarzschild coordinates

concepts.name: Chandrasekhar limit
concepts.definition: The maximum mass, about 1.4 solar masses, of a white dwarf supported by electron degeneracy pressure; heavier remnants collapse further.
concepts.how_introduced: Margin note in the collapse section, with neutron-star and lightest-black-hole masses.

concepts.name: neutron star
concepts.definition: A compact stellar remnant supported mainly by neutron degeneracy and nuclear forces, formed when a core exceeds the Chandrasekhar limit; its maximum mass sets the threshold above which a remnant must be a black hole.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned as the intermediate endpoint and as the benchmark for identifying black holes in X-ray binaries.

concepts.name: closed trapped surface
concepts.definition: A closed spacelike 2-surface from which both the outgoing and ingoing families of orthogonal light rays converge, as happens for spheres of constant r inside the Schwarzschild horizon.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned in passing when noting that light emitted after the stellar surface crosses r_S moves inward in every direction, with a pointer to the next chapter.
prerequisites: exchange of timelike and spacelike roles of t and r inside the horizon

concepts.name: Penrose diagram of a collapse black hole
concepts.definition: A conformally compactified diagram of a spacetime formed by spherical collapse, with r = 0 as a vertical line until a spacelike singularity forms, a 45-degree event horizon reaching i+, and scri-, i0, scri+ bounding the exterior.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalls the Chapter 19 toolkit and presents two diagrams, one schematic and one with the hatched stellar interior, to read off who can see what.

concepts.name: spacelike singularity
concepts.definition: A singularity that forms a spacelike boundary of spacetime, lying to the future of events near it rather than beside them; inside a Schwarzschild horizon r = 0 is such a surface because r is a time coordinate there.
concepts.how_introduced: Read off the Penrose diagram, compared with the t = 0 Big Bang of the Robertson-Walker diagram in Chapter 19.
prerequisites: exchange of timelike and spacelike roles of t and r inside the horizon

concepts.name: supermassive black hole
concepts.definition: A black hole of millions to billions of solar masses at a galactic nucleus, such as Sagittarius A* in the Milky Way.
concepts.how_introduced: Evidence surveyed in Example 25.1: stellar proper motions near Sgr A*, the Event Horizon Telescope image, and quasars.

concepts.name: accretion disc
concepts.definition: A rotating disc of gas spiralling onto a compact object; friction and high orbital speeds heat it enough to radiate strongly, often in X-rays.
concepts.how_introduced: Explained inside Example 25.1 as the source of X-rays from binaries and the energy of quasars.

concepts.name: X-ray binary
concepts.definition: A binary system in which a compact object accretes from a companion star and emits X-rays; if the dynamically measured compact mass exceeds neutron-star limits the object is taken to be a black hole.
concepts.how_introduced: Cygnus X-1 is offered as the classic example in Example 25.1.

concepts.name: quasar
concepts.definition: A very luminous galactic nucleus powered by accretion onto a supermassive black hole, first mistaken for a star.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 25.1 and a margin note on the name.

concepts.name: Event Horizon Telescope image
concepts.definition: A very-long-baseline radio interferometric image of the Galactic Centre black hole showing a dark central shadow inside a bright emission ring.
concepts.how_introduced: Reproduced as Fig. 25.1 in the evidence example, with a caption giving the mass and region size.

concepts.name: black-hole exterior equals stellar exterior
concepts.definition: Outside the horizon a spherical black hole's gravity is identical to that of any spherical star of the same mass, so orbits and escape work as usual unless one crosses r_S.
concepts.how_introduced: Margin note correcting the popular picture of black holes as cosmic vacuum cleaners, justified implicitly by Birkhoff.

concepts.name: Painleve-Gullstrand coordinates
concepts.definition: Coordinates (t-tilde, r, theta, phi) whose time is the proper time of clocks falling radially from rest at infinity; the metric -dT^2 + (dr + (2M/r)^(1/2) dT)^2 + r^2 dOmega^2 is regular at r = 2M and has flat constant-time slices.
concepts.how_introduced: Developed entirely in Exercises 25.1-25.3, first by a transformation dt = dT - R(r) dr and then physically from an array of dropped clocks, with a historical note on Painleve, Gullstrand and Lemaitre.

key_equations.name: Schwarzschild line element
key_equations.meaning: Geometry of empty space around a spherical mass, used here all the way down to r = 0; g_tt vanishes and g_rr diverges at r = 2M.
key_equations.symbols: M mass (geometrized); t, r, theta, phi Schwarzschild coordinates

key_equations.name: Schwarzschild radius in SI units
key_equations.meaning: Size scale of the horizon: about 3 km per solar mass.
key_equations.symbols: G Newton's constant; c speed of light; M_sun about 2e30 kg

key_equations.name: Radial light-cone slope
key_equations.meaning: Edges of radial light cones in the (r, t) plane; slope 1 far away, vertical at r = 2M, so cones close up approaching the horizon.

key_equations.name: Metric just inside the horizon
key_equations.meaning: Schwarzschild metric with r = 2M - epsilon, epsilon > 0: the dt^2 term is now positive (spacelike) and the depsilon^2 term negative (timelike).

key_equations.name: Interval at fixed t, theta, phi inside the horizon
key_equations.meaning: A pure change in r inside the horizon is timelike, so r acts as time and must change monotonically.

key_equations.name: Coordinate-time integral along radial light
key_equations.meaning: Generic integral whose logarithmic piece causes divergent coordinate times at the horizon.

key_equations.name: Definition of the tortoise coordinate
key_equations.meaning: New radial coordinate chosen so that radial light moves at unit coordinate speed.

key_equations.name: Tortoise coordinate
key_equations.meaning: r* agrees with r at large radius and runs to minus infinity as r approaches 2M from outside (Fig. 25.4).

key_equations.name: Radial light rays in tortoise form
key_equations.meaning: Outgoing and ingoing radial null curves are straight 45-degree lines in (r*, t).

key_equations.name: Schwarzschild metric in (t, r*)
key_equations.meaning: Radial part is conformally flat, so light cones keep their 45-degree shape; the horizon is at r* = -infinity.

key_equations.name: Proper time of the radial plunge
key_equations.meaning: Proper time along a fall from rest at infinity is a smooth function of r, finite at r_S and at r = 0. NOTE: the book prints a plus sign before the 2/3 term; the minus sign is required for tau to increase as r decreases and agrees with eqn 22.33 and Fig. 25.5.
key_equations.symbols: tau_* proper time at which r = 0 is reached

key_equations.name: Schwarzschild time of the radial plunge
key_equations.meaning: Distant observers' time for the same fall; the logarithm diverges as r approaches r_S (Fig. 25.6).

key_equations.name: Geodesic deviation in the orthonormal frame (margin note 11)
key_equations.meaning: Relative acceleration of neighbouring free particles set by curvature.
key_equations.symbols: chi separation vector; hats denote orthonormal components

key_equations.name: Schwarzschild orthonormal Riemann components (margin note 11)
key_equations.latex: R_{\hat\tau\hat r\hat\tau\hat r}=-\frac{2M}{r^3},\quad R_{\hat\theta\hat\phi\hat\theta\hat\phi}=\frac{2M}{r^3},\quad R_{\hat\tau\hat\theta\hat\tau\hat\theta}=R_{\hat\tau\hat\phi\hat\tau\hat\phi}=\frac{M}{r^3},\quad R_{\hat r\hat\theta\hat r\hat\theta}=R_{\hat r\hat\phi\hat r\hat\phi}=-\frac{M}{r^3}
key_equations.meaning: All curvature components are finite and smooth at r = 2M and diverge only at r = 0. (The exported text garbles the first index set; the rendered page gives tau-r-tau-r.)

key_equations.name: Tidal accelerations on a falling astronaut
key_equations.meaning: Radial stretching and transverse squeezing with strength M/r^3: unremarkable at r_S, unbounded as r goes to 0.

key_equations.name: Null condition for radial light
key_equations.meaning: Starting point for the travel time of the astronaut's radial light pulses.
Plus sign chosen for outgoing photons.

key_equations.name: Coordinate travel time of an outgoing radial photon
key_equations.meaning: Flat-space delay plus a logarithmic correction that diverges as the emission radius approaches r_S: pulses reach distant observers ever more slowly (Fig. 25.7).
key_equations.symbols: (t1, r1) emission event; (t2, r2) reception event; r1, r2 > r_S

key_equations.name: Critical photon angle
key_equations.meaning: Boundary between captured and escaping (or, by time reversal, visible and dark) directions for a static observer; zero at r = 2M, 90 degrees at r = 3M.
key_equations.symbols: psi_c angle from the radial direction measured in the static observer's frame

key_equations.name: Energy measured by a static observer
key_equations.latex: E_{\rm obs}=p^{\hat t}=(\boldsymbol e_t)^{\hat t}p^t,\qquad(\boldsymbol e_t)^{\hat t}=\left(1-\frac{2M}{r}\right)^{1/2}
key_equations.meaning: Project the photon momentum onto the static orthonormal frame.

key_equations.name: Conservation of p_t for infalling light (margin note 15)
key_equations.meaning: Time-translation symmetry fixes how the coordinate energy component grows inward. (The book drops the sign of g_tt here; magnitudes are what matter.)

key_equations.name: Blueshift of incoming starlight
key_equations.meaning: Static observers deep in the potential see starlight shifted to higher energy; the inverse of the gravitational redshift eqn 22.16.

key_equations.name: Schwarzschild metric with v^2 = 2M/r (Exercise 25.1)
key_equations.meaning: Rewriting that makes v the Newtonian escape (and plunge) speed.
key_equations.symbols: dOmega^2 = dtheta^2 + sin^2 theta dphi^2 (the exercise omits the square on dphi)

key_equations.name: Painleve-Gullstrand metric (Exercise 25.1)
key_equations.meaning: Result of dt = dT - R(r) dr with R = v/(1 - v^2); regular at r = 2M and flat on constant-T slices.

key_equations.latex: d\tilde t=\left(\frac{\partial\tilde t}{\partial t}\right)dt+\left(\frac{\partial\tilde t}{\partial r}\right)dr
key_equations.meaning: Rain time as a function of Schwarzschild t and r.
key_equations.symbols: t-tilde time read on dropped clocks

key_equations.meaning: Clocks dropped at a steady rate make rain time advance with t at fixed r.

key_equations.name: Radial plunge proper speed
key_equations.meaning: Rain clocks fall at the Newtonian escape speed in proper time.

key_equations.name: Radial plunge coordinate speed
key_equations.meaning: Coordinate speed goes to zero at the horizon.
Drop-time interval between neighbouring clocks separated by dr at equal t.

key_equations.name: Proper fall time between two radii
key_equations.meaning: Finite proper time from r_A to r_B for fall from rest at infinity.
Radial dependence of rain time.

key_equations.name: Global rain metric (Exercise 25.3)
key_equations.meaning: Expanded Painleve-Gullstrand form; no component is singular at r = 2M, and its null directions show inward motion inside the horizon.

figures.label: Fig. 25.1
figures.caption_paraphrase: Event Horizon Telescope radio image of Sagittarius A*, a dark shadow inside a bright ring, with about four million solar masses in a region some 0.3 AU across.
figures.visual_description: Square greyscale image on a black background. A blurry, lumpy bright annulus fills the centre, brighter in knots toward the upper right and lower right, surrounding a darker, roughly circular depression slightly off centre. No axes, scale bar or labels.
figures.what_it_teaches: Black holes are inferred from what surrounds them: the visible feature is emission from hot gas and a central deficit of light, not the hole itself.
concepts: apparent angular size of a black hole

redesign.idea: Shadow-size calculator: show a schematic ring whose angular diameter is computed from the capture cross-section (diameter about 2 sqrt(27) GM/c^2 divided by distance) next to the EHT-style blur.
redesign.interaction: Learner picks a target (Sgr A*, M87*, a 10 solar-mass hole at 1 kpc) or enters mass and distance; the ring size in microarcseconds and the resolution needed update, with a telescope-baseline slider showing when the ring becomes resolvable.

figures.label: Fig. 25.2
figures.caption_paraphrase: Light cones get thinner as r falls toward the horizon and are turned on their side inside it.
figures.visual_description: Axes t (up) and r (right) with origin 0 and a dotted vertical line at r_S. A row of hourglass-shaped cones at the same height: the two at the far right are wide with 45-degree edges; moving left toward r_S they become narrower, the one just outside r_S being almost a vertical sliver. Just inside the dotted line a cone is drawn as two overlapping ellipses (caught while tipping), and at the far left a cone lies on its side, its axis parallel to the r axis like a bow tie.
figures.what_it_teaches: Causal structure changes continuously in these coordinates: pinching outside and a 90-degree tip inside mean that the future direction inside the horizon is along r.
concepts: radial light cones in Schwarzschild coordinates
closing of light cones near the horizon
exchange of timelike and spacelike roles of t and r inside the horizon

redesign.idea: Live light-cone probe on an (r, t) diagram computed from dt/dr = +/-(1 - 2M/r)^-1, with a switch to ingoing Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates to show the same cones tilting smoothly instead of pinching.
redesign.interaction: Learner drags an event horizontally through r = 2M; its cone redraws, a readout gives the coordinate light speed and which r-direction is future; a coordinate toggle morphs the diagram between Schwarzschild and EF.

figures.label: Fig. 25.3
figures.caption_paraphrase: Map of radial light rays and light cones drawn in Schwarzschild coordinates.
figures.visual_description: Quarter-plane with t up and r right, origin 0, and a thick dashed vertical line at r_S. Thin grey curves with arrowheads form two crossing families on each side. Near the dashed line the curves bunch together and turn vertical, running up toward the top edge (a brace labelled 'incoming' spans them). To the right, one family climbs toward the upper right, bracketed as 'outgoing', and the other bends toward the dashed line. Inside r_S, curves run between the t axis and the dashed line in an X-shaped lattice. Small cones sit at many crossings: wide and upright far to the right, tall and thin next to r_S, and tilted inside.
figures.what_it_teaches: In Schwarzschild coordinates radial null curves seem to shoot off to infinite t at the horizon on both sides, a coordinate artefact to be removed in Chapter 26.
concepts: radial null geodesics in Schwarzschild spacetime
closing of light cones near the horizon

redesign.idea: Null-curve plotter: exact curves t = +/- r* + const drawn for r > 2M and r < 2M, with photons launched by clicking, shown side by side with the same photons in (r*, t) and ingoing EF coordinates.
redesign.interaction: Learner clicks an event to emit ingoing and outgoing photons; the three panels animate the same two photons; a slider sets how many reference rays are drawn; hovering a curve highlights its counterparts in the other panels.

figures.label: Fig. 25.4
figures.caption_paraphrase: Graph of the tortoise coordinate against r.
figures.visual_description: Axes r* (up) and r (right) with a dotted vertical line labelled 2M. A single solid curve emerges from far below, hugging the dotted line, crosses the r axis a little to the right of 2M, then bends over and rises ever more gently, approaching a straight line of unit slope at large r. Only the region r > 2M is shown.
figures.what_it_teaches: r* tracks r far away but drops to minus infinity at the horizon, so an infinite range of r* is spent approaching 2M.

redesign.idea: Achilles-and-tortoise race tied to the r*(r) graph: a dot moves down the curve at constant speed in r*, while a runner on a track shows r approaching 2M ever more slowly.
redesign.interaction: Learner drags r* or presses play; the runner's distance to the finish line (r - 2M) and the local slope dr/dr* update; an optional toggle reveals the r < 2M branch.

figures.label: Fig. 25.5
figures.caption_paraphrase: Proper time along a radial plunge as a function of r.
figures.visual_description: Axes tau (up) and r (right). The tau axis is drawn as a zigzag, marking the singularity at r = 0, and a dotted vertical line marks r_S. A smooth concave-down solid curve starts on the r axis at the release radius and rises to the left, passing through the dotted line without any feature, and meets the tau axis at a finite height.
figures.what_it_teaches: The traveller reaches the horizon and then the singularity after a finite proper time, with nothing special at r_S.
concepts: proper time versus coordinate time at the horizon

redesign.idea: Two-clock plunge: an animated astronaut falls along r while two synchronized plots trace tau(r) and t(r) (merging Figs. 25.5 and 25.6), with her torch pulses sent at equal proper-time intervals and their arrival times at a distant observer marked on a timeline.
redesign.interaction: Learner sets starting radius (or fall from infinity) and pulse interval, presses play, and scrubs; the distant timeline shows the pulse gaps widening while her own clock ticks evenly; a readout gives remaining proper time to r = 0 in seconds for a chosen mass.

figures.label: Fig. 25.6
figures.caption_paraphrase: Schwarzschild coordinate time along the same plunge.
figures.visual_description: Axes t (up) and r (right) with a dotted vertical line at r_S. A solid curve starts on the r axis at the same release radius, rises leftward almost linearly, then steepens sharply into a vertical asymptote just outside r_S. Between the t axis and the dotted line a short dashed hook starts at a finite t on the axis, sags slightly, and then climbs up the asymptote on the inner side.
figures.what_it_teaches: Distant-observer time diverges at the horizon although the fall continues; the separate dashed interior piece shows the Schwarzschild chart splitting the trajectory in two.
concepts: proper time versus coordinate time at the horizon
logarithmic divergence of coordinate time at the horizon

redesign.idea: Merged with Fig. 25.5 in the two-clock plunge demo; separately, a log-scale view of t - t_* against r - r_S reveals the logarithmic divergence as a straight line.
redesign.interaction: Learner toggles linear or logarithmic axes and zooms into the region near r_S to see the divergence rate.

figures.label: Fig. 25.7
figures.caption_paraphrase: Photon coordinate travel time against reception radius for three emission radii.
figures.visual_description: Axes Delta t (up) and r2 (right). Three rising curves, labelled 1.1 r_S, 2 r_S and 5 r_S, each start at Delta t = 0 where r2 equals its emission radius, so they begin progressively further right. The 1.1 r_S curve shoots up steeply at first and then bends to a steadier slope; the 2 r_S curve starts less steeply; the 5 r_S curve is nearly a straight line.
figures.what_it_teaches: The closer to r_S a signal is emitted, the larger the logarithmic extra delay, which dominates the flat-space r2 - r1 term near the horizon.
concepts: radial null geodesics in Schwarzschild spacetime
apparent freezing and redshifting of infalling sources

redesign.idea: Delay decomposition plot: for a draggable emission radius, show the flat-space delay and the logarithmic term as stacked areas, plus the arrival time at a fixed far detector.
redesign.interaction: Learner slides r1 from 10 r_S down toward r_S and watches the logarithmic slice balloon; a counter reports how many extra hours or microseconds the delay adds for a chosen black-hole mass.

figures.label: Fig. 25.8
figures.caption_paraphrase: Collapse of a star in the (r, t) plane with angular directions suppressed; each point stands for a sphere.
figures.visual_description: Axes t (up) and r (right). A hatched region, the star's interior, is bounded by the t axis and a thick curve that starts on the r axis at the initial radius and bows inward and upward to reach r = 0 at a finite t. Above that point a wavy line along the t axis is labelled 'singularity'. A thick vertical line labelled r = 2M rises from where the stellar surface crosses 2M. Four small cone sketches float in the empty region: upright far outside, slightly tilted just outside the line, strongly tilted inward just inside it, and tipped toward the singularity near the axis.
figures.what_it_teaches: Once the surface passes r = 2M, a horizon exists outside the remaining matter and all future cones inside point toward the singularity.
concepts: exchange of timelike and spacelike roles of t and r inside the horizon

redesign.idea: Collapse diagram drawn in ingoing Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates from an Oppenheimer-Snyder dust model, with light emitted from the surface at chosen moments.
redesign.interaction: Learner scrubs the surface's proper time; flashes emitted radially outward are traced, coloured by whether they reach a distant observer, and the horizon line appears at the moment the escaping-light boundary forms, which is before the surface reaches 2M.

figures.label: Fig. 25.9
figures.caption_paraphrase: Stellar collapse drawn in three dimensions, suppressing one space direction.
figures.visual_description: Hand-drawn 3D sketch: a flared, bell-shaped surface with faint internal dashed lines, representing the star's shrinking surface, narrows upward and merges into a vertical cylinder (the horizon). A wavy vertical line inside the cylinder marks the singularity. Small cone-shaped cups are scattered around: those far away stand upright, those near the cylinder tilt toward its axis, and those on or inside it lean over strongly.
figures.what_it_teaches: The horizon is a tube in spacetime that the star's worldtube enters, and cones progressively tip inward as one approaches it.
concepts: radial light cones in Schwarzschild coordinates

redesign.idea: Orbitable 3D worldtube of a collapsing star with a horizon cylinder and computed light cones on a grid (EF coordinates), each cone coloured by whether any of its outgoing rays can escape.
redesign.interaction: Learner rotates and zooms, moves a probe cone around, and scrubs time to watch the horizon cylinder grow out from the centre and the star's surface pass through it.

figures.label: Fig. 25.10
figures.caption_paraphrase: Penrose diagram of spacetime containing a black hole with event horizon H.
figures.visual_description: Axes labelled t' (vertical) and r' (horizontal). The left boundary is the vertical axis r = 0, running up from i- at the bottom. A straight edge scri- rises at 45 degrees from i- to i0 on the right, and scri+ runs back up-left from i0 to i+. A short horizontal double line near the top of the axis, ending at i+, marks the singularity. A short dotted 45-degree segment labelled H climbs from just below the singularity toward i+, cutting off a thin triangular interior region beneath the double line. No stellar matter is drawn.
figures.what_it_teaches: The singularity is a spacelike line at the top, the horizon is the null boundary of what can signal to scri+, and everything above H ends on the singularity.
concepts: Penrose diagram of a collapse black hole

redesign.idea: Clickable Penrose diagram: each click draws the future light cone of the chosen event as 45-degree lines and colours the event by whether its cone reaches scri+, so the horizon emerges as the dividing line rather than being drawn in.
redesign.interaction: Learner clicks or drags an event; its future cone updates; a 'paint' mode shades every tested event, revealing the interior triangle; a toggle overlays lines of constant Schwarzschild r and t.

figures.label: Fig. 25.11
figures.caption_paraphrase: Penrose diagram of a star collapsing to form a black hole, with the stellar matter hatched.
figures.visual_description: Thick outline: a vertical left edge (the centre r = 0) rising from a bottom vertex; a thick horizontal top edge labelled 'singularity'; a thick edge scri+ descending from the top-right corner to i0 on the right; and scri- returning from i0 to the bottom vertex. A hatched region labelled 'fluid' lies against the left edge, bounded by a curve that leaves the bottom vertex, bulges to the right, and curves back to meet the singularity near its left end. A thick 45-degree line labelled H runs from the fluid boundary to the top-right corner. The unhatched area is labelled 'empty space'.
figures.what_it_teaches: The star's surface crosses the horizon and ends on the singularity, while the exterior beyond the horizon is ordinary empty space connected to infinity.
concepts: Penrose diagram of a collapse black hole

redesign.idea: Animated collapse on the Penrose diagram: the stellar surface worldline is traced while an outside observer's worldline receives the surface's light signals, which pile up along H.
redesign.interaction: Learner scrubs a slider for the observer's proper time and sees the last received image; a second slider moves the emission event on the stellar surface, showing when its light first fails to reach scri+.

worked_examples.label: Example 25.1
worked_examples.problem: Summarize the observational case that black holes exist even though they emit no light.
worked_examples.method: Qualitative survey organised by the kind of evidence: stellar dynamics at the Galactic Centre, dynamical masses of X-ray-emitting binaries, compact energetic galactic nuclei, and gravitational-wave signals.
worked_examples.key_insight: All the evidence is indirect: a mass too large and too compact for any known stellar remnant, betrayed by its effect on stars, gas or spacetime ripples.
worked_examples.result: Sgr A* about 4e6 solar masses; Cygnus X-1 about 15 solar masses in a source smaller than a few hundred km; quasar ULAS J1342+0928 about 8e8 solar masses.

worked_examples.label: Example 25.2
worked_examples.problem: Give an intuition for why r* is called the tortoise coordinate.
worked_examples.method: Cast the approach to the horizon as Zeno's race: Achilles' gap to the tortoise is r - r_S, and r* serves as a race clock that runs downward; use dr/dr* = 1 - 2M/r to show the closing speed dies away.
worked_examples.key_insight: Arbitrarily large decreases in r* buy ever smaller progress in r, so the horizon corresponds to r* = -infinity and is never reached in this label.
worked_examples.result: r approaches 2M only asymptotically as r* goes to minus infinity.
concepts: coordinates have no intrinsic metric meaning

worked_examples.label: Example 25.3
worked_examples.problem: What does an astronaut falling radially into the hole physically feel?
worked_examples.method: Take the geodesic deviation equation in the orthonormal frame with the Schwarzschild Riemann components (from Chapter 11) to get relative accelerations along r-hat, theta-hat and phi-hat.
worked_examples.key_insight: The tidal field depends on M/r^3 only, so it is finite at r_S; it stretches radially and compresses sideways and grows without bound as r goes to 0, where the true singularity lies.
worked_examples.result: d^2chi^r/dtau^2 = (2M/r^3) chi^r; transverse components get -(M/r^3) chi.
concepts: Riemann tensor in the static orthonormal frame

worked_examples.label: Example 25.4
worked_examples.problem: How much of the sky does the black hole block for an observer at r = 3M, and what happens closer in?
worked_examples.method: Evaluate the critical angle formula at r = 3M and note its trend as r decreases toward 2M.
worked_examples.key_insight: At the photon-orbit radius the critical angle is a right angle, so the dark region is exactly a hemisphere; deeper in, the visible universe contracts to a narrowing cone.
worked_examples.result: sin psi_c = 1, psi_c = pi/2: black hole fills half the sky; tangential light returns to the emitter.
concepts: apparent angular size of a black hole

worked_examples.problem: Show that inside r = 2M the radial coordinate is timelike.
worked_examples.method: Substitute r = 2M - epsilon into the Schwarzschild metric, then set dt = dtheta = dphi = 0 and inspect the sign of ds^2.
worked_examples.key_insight: The metric coefficients of dt^2 and dr^2 swap sign at r = 2M, so the coordinate that must advance monotonically along any worldline inside is r, not t.
worked_examples.result: ds^2 = -(2M - epsilon) depsilon^2/epsilon < 0 at fixed t: epsilon must increase, r must decrease.
concepts: exchange of timelike and spacelike roles of t and r inside the horizon
inevitability of reaching r = 0 inside the horizon

worked_examples.problem: Integrate the tortoise coordinate and rewrite the metric in terms of it.
worked_examples.method: Split 1/(1 - 2M/r) = 1 + 2M/(r - 2M) and integrate; then replace dr by (1 - 2M/r) dr* in the metric.
worked_examples.key_insight: Radial null lines become t = +/- r* + const and the (t, r*) metric is a conformal factor times flat space, but the factor vanishes where r* goes to minus infinity.
worked_examples.result: r* = r + 2M ln|r/2M - 1| + const; ds^2 = (1 - 2M/r)(-dt^2 + dr*^2) + r^2 dOmega^2.
concepts: conformally flat form of the radial Schwarzschild metric

worked_examples.problem: How long, in Schwarzschild time, does an outgoing radial light pulse take from r1 to r2?
worked_examples.method: Take the plus root of the radial null condition and integrate dr/(1 - r_S/r) between the two radii.
worked_examples.key_insight: The answer is the flat-space distance plus r_S times a logarithm; as the emission point approaches r_S the logarithm, and so the delay, diverges.
concepts: radial null geodesics in Schwarzschild spacetime
apparent freezing and redshifting of infalling sources

worked_examples.problem: Find the energy of starlight measured by a static observer at radius r.
worked_examples.method: Use conservation of p_t to get p^t(r) from the frequency at infinity, then project with the static vielbein component (e_t)^t-hat = (1 - 2M/r)^(1/2).
worked_examples.key_insight: Two factors of (1 - 2M/r) combine to leave a net inverse square root, the redshift law run backwards.
worked_examples.result: E_obs = hbar omega_inf (1 - 2M/r)^(-1/2), diverging at the horizon.
concepts: measured energy from the orthonormal frame

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: The horizon of the Earth beyond which ships vanish from view
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Supplies the name: just as we cannot see past the Earth's curvature, no event inside r = 2M can be seen from outside.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The Earth's horizon depends on where the observer stands and can be crossed and seen past by moving; the black-hole horizon is a null surface fixed by the spacetime, and once inside, no signal can ever get out.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Side-by-side: a ship sinking below a horizon that rises back into view when the observer climbs a mast, versus a photon inside r = 2M that stays hidden whatever the observer does.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Achilles chasing the tortoise in Zeno's paradox
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Treats r - r_S as the gap Achilles must close and r* as a clock that can be run down forever; the gap shrinks ever more slowly, so the finish is never reached in r*.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: In Zeno the paradox is resolved because the infinite steps take finite time; likewise the horizon is reached in finite proper time. The analogy's 'never reaches' is only true of the r* label, which the book says but a learner may miss.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Race animation with two clocks: the r* clock ticks forever while a proper-time clock for an infalling runner reaches the line in a finite count.

analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Gives a vivid image for radial elongation and sideways squeezing from eqn 25.12.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Only describes the pattern; how early it becomes lethal depends strongly on mass (fatal outside the horizon for stellar holes, negligible at the horizon of supermassive ones).
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: A deformable astronaut figure that stretches and squeezes according to 2M/r^3 and M/r^3 times body size, with a mass slider showing where stretching exceeds bodily tolerance relative to r_S.

analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: exchange of timelike and spacelike roles of t and r inside the horizon
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Condenses the sign-flip calculation into a slogan: inside the horizon, decreasing r is as unavoidable as tomorrow.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Can suggest that r = 0 is a point in space one is pulled toward; it is better thought of as a moment in the future, as the spacelike singularity on the Penrose diagram shows.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Calendar metaphor: inside the horizon, a slider labelled 'r' can only be moved one way, just as a date slider only advances.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: After crossing r = 2M the star is effectively cut off, as though it had left for a separate universe
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Emphasizes that after crossing the horizon the stellar matter can no longer influence the outside, which only feels the horizon and exterior geometry.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The interior is not a separate universe: its mass and (for other holes) charge and spin remain imprinted on the exterior, and outside matter can still fall in.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Michell and Laplace's dark star whose escape speed exceeds light speed
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Historical margin note locating the idea before general relativity.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Newtonian light could climb above the surface and fall back and could be seen by nearby observers; in GR nothing inside the horizon even moves outward, and the radius coincidence with 2GM/c^2 hides different physics.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Compare the Newtonian escape-speed radius with the GR horizon: launch a light pulse outward from just inside each and watch the Newtonian one rise and fall while the GR one moves inward.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: A variable called t has no more claim to be time than one called u or chi
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: coordinates have no intrinsic metric meaning
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Defuses the shock that t becomes spacelike inside the horizon: names of coordinates do not determine their causal character; the metric does.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Not an analogy so much as a principle; learners still need the sign test on metric coefficients to apply it.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Something dramatic, such as an infinite force or a wall, happens to a traveller at r = 2M because the metric blows up there.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Curvature components and tidal accelerations are finite and smooth at r = 2M and the traveller's clock ticks normally; the divergence belongs to the Schwarzschild coordinates.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: g_rr is literally infinite in the formula and coordinate time to reach r_S is infinite.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A black hole sucks in everything around it like a cosmic vacuum cleaner.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Outside the horizon its gravity is exactly that of any spherical star of the same mass; orbits are stable and a rocket can always leave as long as it never crosses r_S.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Popular accounts stress that nothing escapes, which is only true inside the horizon.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Since distant observers never see the astronaut cross, she never actually crosses the horizon.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Her proper time to cross and to reach r = 0 is finite; the apparent freezing is due to signals from near r_S taking unboundedly long in Schwarzschild time to climb out.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Coordinate time is the distant observer's real clock, so its divergence feels like a physical statement.
concepts: proper time versus coordinate time at the horizon
apparent freezing and redshifting of infalling sources

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The coordinate named t always measures time.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Inside the horizon t is a spacelike coordinate and r is timelike; only the sign of the metric along a displacement decides its character.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Outside, and in flat spacetime, t really is time for static observers.
concepts: exchange of timelike and spacelike roles of t and r inside the horizon
coordinates have no intrinsic metric meaning

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: With a powerful enough rocket, an astronaut just inside the horizon could hover or climb back out.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Inside, every future-pointing light cone points toward smaller r; even light fired outward moves inward, and no worldline can stay at constant r.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Outside the horizon, thrust can counter gravity at any radius, and the horizon looks like an ordinary sphere.
concepts: inevitability of reaching r = 0 inside the horizon

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The singularity r = 0 is a point at the centre of space that a clever trajectory could steer around.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Inside the horizon r = 0 is a spacelike surface lying in every infalling observer's future, like a final moment of time; the Penrose diagram draws it as a horizontal line.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: In the exterior r = 0 would be the spatial centre, and the phrase 'infinitely dense point at the origin' reinforces that picture.
concepts: exchange of timelike and spacelike roles of t and r inside the horizon

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Distant astronomers could eventually watch a star collapse through its horizon or see the singularity.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The star's image slows, reddens and fades as its surface nears r_S; light from inside never gets out, so the singularity stays hidden.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Given enough patience, one expects to see every stage of a process.
concepts: apparent freezing and redshifting of infalling sources

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The tortoise coordinate removes the horizon problem.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: It keeps radial light rays at 45 degrees and the metric finite, but it moves r = 2M to r* = -infinity, so the horizon and interior are still unreachable in the chart.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The metric in (t, r*) looks as clean as flat space.
concepts: conformally flat form of the radial Schwarzschild metric

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The Event Horizon Telescope photographed the black hole itself or its event horizon.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The image shows radio emission from hot gas around the hole, with a central brightness deficit (the shadow) whose size is set by photon capture near r = 3M, larger than the horizon.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The caption calls it an image of the black hole and the telescope is named after the horizon.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The half-sky view at 3M and the final chink of blue light describe what a freely falling astronaut sees.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Those results use static-observer frames. A falling observer moving inward suffers aberration and Doppler shift, so the hole looks smaller and starlight is less blueshifted than for a hovering observer at the same r.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The section is narrated as the plunging astronaut's view, while a margin note quietly says the vielbein is that of a stationary observer.
concepts: apparent angular size of a black hole
measured energy from the orthonormal frame

thought_experiments.name: Astronaut with a torch falling into a black hole
thought_experiments.setup: An astronaut falls radially from rest far away and flashes a light at regular intervals of her own time toward distant observers.
