thought_experiments.lesson: She crosses the horizon and meets the singularity in finite proper time, feeling growing tidal forces but nothing at r_S; outside observers receive ever more widely spaced, dimmer, redder pulses and never see the crossing.
concepts: proper time versus coordinate time at the horizon
apparent freezing and redshifting of infalling sources
thought_experiments.app_idea: Split-screen: her cockpit view with a steady clock and stretching body on one side, the distant telescope feed with slowing, reddening flashes on the other.

thought_experiments.name: Photon fired outward from inside the horizon
thought_experiments.setup: An astronaut already inside r = 2M shines a light in the outward radial direction.
thought_experiments.lesson: Because the cone is tipped over, the outward-aimed photon still moves to smaller r; nothing inside can escape or be seen.
concepts: exchange of timelike and spacelike roles of t and r inside the horizon
inevitability of reaching r = 0 inside the horizon
thought_experiments.app_idea: Photon launcher on an EF diagram: aim left or right from any event and see whether r ever increases.

thought_experiments.name: Achilles and the tortoise race timed by r*
thought_experiments.setup: Achilles' distance from the tortoise is r - r_S and the race clock reads r*, run downward without limit.
thought_experiments.lesson: In the r* label the gap closes ever more slowly and the finish is at r* = -infinity, which is why the horizon is inaccessible in tortoise coordinates.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Animated runners with an r* counter and a proper-time counter to show both views.

thought_experiments.name: Seeing the back of your head at r = 3M
thought_experiments.setup: An observer at the photon-orbit radius emits light exactly tangentially.
thought_experiments.lesson: The light circles the hole and returns, so the observer would see herself from behind; the same radius marks where the hole fills half the sky.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Ray-traced first-person view for a static observer with a radius slider, showing the dark region grow and a ring image of the observer at 3M.

thought_experiments.name: Watching a star collapse
thought_experiments.setup: Distant astronomers monitor the surface of a massive star whose core collapses through r = 2M.
thought_experiments.lesson: The image slows, reddens and blackens as the surface nears r_S; afterwards only the horizon and exterior geometry matter to outsiders, and the singularity stays hidden.
concepts: apparent freezing and redshifting of infalling sources
thought_experiments.app_idea: Light curve and colour of a collapsing star's surface versus distant-observer time, computed from outgoing null rays, with the curve approaching zero exponentially.

historical_notes.event: Proposed dark stars so compact that the escape speed from their surface would exceed the speed of light.
historical_notes.significance: Pre-relativistic precursor of the black-hole idea, with a radius numerically matching 2GM/c^2.

historical_notes.event: Published the key calculation of continued gravitational collapse of a massive star, following late-1930s work on neutron-star collapse.
historical_notes.significance: First GR demonstration that collapse can produce what is now called a black hole.
Marks the period when black holes became mainstream physics.

historical_notes.event: Einstein jokingly called the Schwarzschild radius singularity the 'Hadamard catastrophe', after Hadamard suggested it might be physically real.
historical_notes.significance: Shows early uncertainty about whether r = 2M is physical, the question this chapter and the next resolve.

historical_notes.event: Computed that white dwarfs above about 1.4 solar masses cannot support themselves against collapse.
historical_notes.significance: Sets the threshold above which stellar remnants become neutron stars or black holes.

historical_notes.event: Painlevé (a mathematician who was twice French Prime Minister) and Gullstrand (1911 Nobel laureate in physiology or medicine) independently wrote down a spherically symmetric line element regular at r = 2M and took it as a sign that GR admitted too many solutions; Lemaître showed in 1933 that it is just Schwarzschild in new coordinates. The exercise note adds that Gullstrand, doubting relativity, stood in the way of a Nobel Prize for Einstein's relativity work.
historical_notes.significance: An early concrete case of mistaking a coordinate change for new physics, and the historical root of the 'rain' coordinates built in the exercises. Painlevé's paper is usually dated 1921, and Einstein's 1921 prize cited the photoelectric effect, so the book's compressed anecdote should be told with care.

historical_notes.event: Released the radio image of the shadow of Sagittarius A*, obtained by linking radio observatories across Earth.
historical_notes.significance: Direct imaging of the environment of the Milky Way's central black hole.

applications_and_observations.details: Restoring G and c gives the horizon size for a given mass.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: r_S about 3 km per solar mass; M_sun about 2e30 kg.

applications_and_observations.details: Compact radio source at the Galactic Centre, weighed by the orbits of nearby stars and imaged by the EHT. Our own estimate: r_S about 1.2e7 km (0.08 AU), and the capture shadow diameter of about 5.2 r_S is roughly 0.4 AU, consistent in scale with the 0.3 AU region quoted.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Mass about 4e6 solar masses within a region about 0.3 AU across (book); r_S about 0.08 AU (our estimate).

applications_and_observations.details: X-ray binary with the blue supergiant HDE 226868; companion motion fixes the unseen mass, too large for a neutron star; X-rays come from a hot accretion disc.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Book: about 15 solar masses, source diameter below several hundred km. Later (2021) analyses revised the mass to about 21 solar masses.

applications_and_observations.details: Extremely luminous accreting supermassive black holes at galactic centres, with high redshifts and jets.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: ULAS J1342+0928 black hole about 8e8 solar masses (book); its 'most distant' status has since been overtaken.

applications_and_observations.details: Listed as the fourth line of evidence, deferred to Chapter 46.
White-dwarf limit, heaviest known neutron star and lightest black holes bracket the collapse outcomes.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Chandrasekhar limit about 1.4 solar masses; heaviest neutron star about 2.4; lightest black hole about 4 (book values, evolving with new data).

applications_and_observations.topic: Tidal stretching at the horizon versus mass (our own estimate)
applications_and_observations.details: Radial tidal acceleration gradient 2GM/r^3 evaluated at r = 2GM/c^2 equals c^6/(4G^2M^2), so heavier holes are gentler at the horizon.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Our estimate: about 1e8 s^-2 for 10 solar masses (lethal for a 2 m body well outside r_S) versus about 6e-4 s^-2 for 4e6 solar masses (unnoticeable at the horizon).

applications_and_observations.topic: Proper time from horizon to singularity (our own estimate)
applications_and_observations.details: For a fall from rest at infinity, eqn 22.33 between r = 2M and 0 gives 4M/3, that is (4/3)GM/c^3.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Our estimate: about 6.6 microseconds per solar mass, so about 66 microseconds for 10 solar masses and about 26 s for Sgr A*.

margin_notes.summary: History of the idea: Michell and Laplace's dark stars, Oppenheimer's late-1930s collapse work culminating in the 1939 Oppenheimer-Snyder paper, and Wheeler's later coining of the popular name.
The r_S surface is a sphere in space (sometimes drawn as a ring on the page); Einstein nicknamed its singularity after Hadamard, who thought it might be real.
Clarifies 'infinite redshift': the received frequency drops to zero, since a single wave cycle would need unbounded time to arrive.
Black holes are not cosmic vacuum cleaners: their exterior is like any star's, and escape is always possible until one crosses r_S.
The word quasar abbreviates quasi-stellar radio source; energetics, redshifts and jets rule out a stellar nature.
Reminder from Chapter 22 that coordinate time and the infaller's proper time differ greatly.
The flip of t to spacelike illustrates that coordinate names carry no metric meaning.
Joke that the section should be titled 'Inside and after the surface' since inside, r is the future.
Achilles in Homer, film and rock music, and why Zeno cast him against a tortoise.
Because coordinates lack metric meaning, the book does not interpret what the r* 'race clock' physically measures.
Geodesic deviation equation in the orthonormal frame and the full list of Schwarzschild orthonormal Riemann components, noting nothing special at r = 2M.
The static-observer redshift formula 22.16 does not apply to a falling emitter; the correct redshift is postponed to the next chapter's coordinates.
At r = 3M tangential light orbits and returns, so an observer could see the back of her head.
Projecting momentum on the static vielbein is the same as the E = -p.u_obs rule; the standard vielbein is a stationary observer's frame.
Derivation of p^t(r) for infalling light from conservation of p_t.
Chandrasekhar limit and the observed mass gap between the heaviest neutron star (about 2.4 solar masses) and the lightest black hole (about 4).

reading causal structure and flat spatial slices off a non-diagonal metric
reusing radial-plunge results (dr/dtau, dr/dt, proper fall time)
building a coordinate system operationally from an array of freely falling clocks
using null directions of a metric to prove inward motion inside a horizon
relating locally measured speeds to conserved energy and angular momentum via u.v = -gamma
deciding capture versus escape with the effective-potential picture

notable.summary: Rewrite Schwarzschild with v^2 = 2M/r, shift the time coordinate by a function of r so the radial metric component becomes one, obtain the Painleve-Gullstrand form, then examine constant-time slices, plunge speeds, light-cone behaviour and the fact that infallers stay slower than light in these coordinates.
notable.why_notable: Gives the reader a working horizon-regular coordinate system before Chapter 26, and shows the constant-time slices are flat Euclidean space. The needed choice is R = v/(1 - v^2).

notable.summary: Construct rain time physically: clocks dropped from rest at infinity at a steady rate, each carrying an observer who records events; derive the partial derivatives of rain time with respect to t and r from plunge kinematics, drop intervals and proper fall times.
skills: partial derivatives of a coordinate map
notable.why_notable: Turns a formal coordinate change into a physical measurement protocol, following Moore and Taylor-Wheeler-Bertschinger; a strong model for demo design.

notable.summary: Combine the results of 25.2 into the expanded rain metric and use it to argue that timelike worldlines inside the horizon must move inward.
skills: assembling a metric from coordinate derivatives
notable.why_notable: Recovers the 'future is inwards' conclusion in coordinates that cover the horizon smoothly, closing the loop with §25.1.

notable.summary: A particle is launched tangentially at speed v0 (as measured by a static observer) at radius r; find its Schwarzschild four-velocity, its conserved energy and angular momentum per unit mass, and decide whether v0 = 1/sqrt(2) at r = 4M prevents capture.
skills: relative velocity from four-velocity dot products
notable.why_notable: Our own check: E-tilde = (1 - 2M/r)^(1/2) gamma and L-tilde = r gamma v0 give E-tilde = 1 and L-tilde = 4M at r = 4M, which is exactly the marginally bound unstable circular orbit of Chapter 23, so the particle balances on a knife edge. The book points to Blennow and Ohlsson.

difficulty.notes: The algebra is light: one-line substitutions, a logarithmic integral and results imported from Chapters 11, 22 and 24. The difficulty is conceptual: accepting that coordinates can swap causal roles, holding finite proper time and infinite coordinate time in mind at once, and reading Penrose diagrams of collapse. Several results are quoted rather than derived (plunge formulas, critical angle, Riemann components), a sign is misprinted in eqn 25.10, and the viewpoint in §25.4 slides between static and falling observers, which can confuse careful readers. The exercises on rain coordinates are noticeably harder than the chapter text.

Radial plunge results quoted for the astronaut: proper time tau(r) (eqn 22.33) and Schwarzschild time t(r) (eqn 22.36); also the earlier point that any radius is reached in finite proper time.
Gravitational redshift eqn 22.16 and the E = -p.u_obs rule; used for blueshift and flagged as inapplicable to falling emitters.
Orthonormal-frame geodesic deviation and Schwarzschild tidal components used in Example 25.3.
Static observer's vielbein used to project photon momentum.

Critical photon angle (eqn 25.16) and the time-reversal reading of it are both taken from §24.2 'Looking around', which ends by promising their consequence for black holes; the text calls it 'the previous chapter'.
Penrose diagrams and conformal structure; spacelike singularity compared with the Robertson-Walker t = 0 surface (§19.3).
Unstable circular orbit at r = 4M with L-tilde = 4M, relevant to Exercise 25.4 (link noted by us).
Classification of singularities, Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates that make the horizon regular, closed trapped surfaces, and the exponential redshift of a falling emitter.
Kruskal-Szekeres coordinates and a fuller Penrose diagram of the Schwarzschild geometry.

teaching_gems.gem: Freeze three coordinates and test the sign of ds^2 along the fourth: inside the horizon a step in r alone is timelike.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Replaces a mysterious slogan with a check any learner can do in two lines, and generalizes to every metric they will meet.
teaching_gems.app_idea: 'Causal character tester': learner picks a metric and a point, chooses a coordinate direction, and a gauge shows the sign of g along it as timelike, null or spacelike; dragging the point across r = 2M flips the gauge for t and r simultaneously.

teaching_gems.gem: Plot the same fall against proper time and against coordinate time side by side.
teaching_gems.why_effective: The contrast between a curve that sails through r_S and one that runs up an asymptote makes the coordinate origin of the divergence visually obvious.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Linked tau(r) and t(r) plots with a shared scrubber and an animated faller; pulses at equal tau intervals are mapped to arrival times at infinity.

teaching_gems.gem: Let tidal stretching decide whether a singularity is real: smooth M/r^3 at r_S, blow-up at r = 0.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Grounds the abstract distinction between coordinate and curvature singularities in something the traveller's body would feel.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Stretch meter for an astronaut of adjustable height falling into holes of adjustable mass, with the horizon and a 'pain threshold' marked on the r axis.

teaching_gems.gem: Drawing a row of light cones that thin out and then fall over as r decreases.
teaching_gems.why_effective: A single strip of pictures carries the whole causal story of the chapter: slowing coordinate speed outside, trapping inside.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Draggable cone along the r axis with computed shape, plus a toggle to Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates where the same cones tilt smoothly.

teaching_gems.gem: Read the photon travel time as flat-space delay plus a logarithm, and show the logarithm taking over as emission approaches r_S.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Splitting the answer into a familiar piece and a GR correction explains the freezing image quantitatively and reuses the tortoise logarithm.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Stacked-bar delay plot with a draggable emission radius and a real-mass clock readout.

teaching_gems.gem: Turn a photon-escape formula into a view of the sky with time reversal, giving a black hole that fills half the sky at 3M.
teaching_gems.why_effective: The setup was planted in Chapter 24, so the payoff costs one evaluation (r = 3M) yet delivers a vivid picture; it also models how a symmetry argument turns an emission result into a reception result.
teaching_gems.app_idea: First-person sky renderer for a static observer (with an optional falling-observer aberration toggle) and a radius slider.

teaching_gems.gem: Naming r* after Zeno's race so that 'approaches but never reaches in this label' is memorable.
teaching_gems.why_effective: A cultural hook attaches to exactly the asymptotic property that matters.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Race animation linked to the r*(r) graph with both an r* counter and a proper-time counter.

teaching_gems.gem: Build horizon-regular coordinates from a physical array of clocks dropped from infinity (Exercise 25.2).
teaching_gems.why_effective: Shows that a coordinate system can be defined by an experiment, which demystifies coordinate changes and previews the next chapter.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Rain-clock simulator: release clocks at a steady rate, watch them fall through r = 2M, and read off the rain-time grid that becomes the Painleve-Gullstrand chart.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Eqn 25.10 is printed with a plus sign, tau = tau_* + (2/3) r^(3/2)/r_S^(1/2), which would make proper time decrease during infall.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners checking against Fig. 25.5 or eqn 22.33 will find a contradiction and may doubt their understanding.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Use tau = tau_* - (2/3) r^(3/2)/r_S^(1/2), with tau_* the time of reaching r = 0, and point out the misprint.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Section 25.4 narrates the plunging astronaut's view but uses the critical angle and blueshift for static observers; a margin note concedes the vielbein is stationary.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners conclude that a freely falling astronaut sees the sky shrink to a tiny blue dot at the horizon, which is not correct once aberration and Doppler shift are included.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: State explicitly that these results are for an observer hovering at r; if possible show the falling observer's view (aberrated sky, finite shift at the horizon) as a contrast.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The critical-angle formula is quoted without saying from which direction psi_c is measured or which of psi_c and pi - psi_c bounds the visible region above and below r = 3M.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Applying 'angles less than psi_c are visible' at r > 3M gives the wrong answer (the hole would seem to cover most of the sky far away).
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Define psi measured from the inward radial direction for the dark patch: at r > 3M the hole's angular radius is psi_c, at r < 3M it is pi - psi_c; check both limits.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Loose or confusing statements about the singularity: a margin note calls r_S a 'shell of singularities' and 'ring-like', and the text says the mass sits at an infinitely dense point.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: 'Ring singularity' is the Kerr term, r_S is not a singularity of spacetime, and picturing r = 0 as a point clashes with the later spacelike-singularity picture.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Say that the coordinate breakdown happens on the sphere r = 2M, reserve 'ring' for Kerr, and describe r = 0 as a final moment rather than a place.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Smoothness of curvature at r = 2M is supported only by frame components in a margin note; no invariant is given.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Sceptical learners may object that components in a frame that itself becomes singular (static observers cannot exist at r <= 2M) prove little.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Add the Kretschmann scalar R_abcd R^abcd = 48M^2/r^6, finite at 2M and infinite at 0, and note that the radial-boost invariance of the tidal components carries them to infalling frames.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The Fig. 25.3 discussion of null curves 'shooting off to infinite t and returning' is terse, and the interior branches are not explained.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Readers can't tell which curves are ingoing or outgoing inside r_S or how a single photon's path is split across the two charts.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Plot t = +/- r* + const explicitly on both sides and then show the same rays in ingoing EF coordinates, where ingoing rays are straight lines through the horizon.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Typos and slips: the singularity written as r_S = 0 in §25.5; 'Painleve-Gullstand'; dOmega^2 missing the square on dphi in Exercise 25.1; §25.3 refers to 'the last chapter' for Chapter 22 results and §25.4 to 'the previous chapter' for Chapter 24.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Minor confusion and hunting for the wrong reference.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Correct to r = 0, Gullstrand, sin^2 theta dphi^2, and cite chapters by number.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Observational numbers are dated: Cygnus X-1's mass has been revised to about 21 solar masses (2021), the most distant quasar record has moved beyond ULAS J1342+0928, the first EHT image (M87*, 2019) is not mentioned, and gravitational-wave events have found compact objects in the claimed 2.4-4 solar-mass gap.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may quote superseded figures or think the mass gap is firm.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Keep book values as illustrative but attach dates, and let the app pull current values for mass estimates and records.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The stellar-evolution story implies that stars above 1.4 solar masses collapse, conflating the initial stellar mass with the remnant core mass.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may believe the Sun's heavier siblings (say 3 solar masses) become black holes, whereas most stars below about 8 solar masses shed mass and end as white dwarfs.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Distinguish initial mass from core or remnant mass and give rough initial-mass ranges for white dwarf, neutron star and black-hole outcomes.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Fig. 25.10 is introduced in the text as the conformal structure produced by collapse, yet it draws no stellar matter (that appears only in Fig. 25.11), and its horizon line H begins below the singularity without comment on when a horizon forms.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may think the horizon appears only when the surface crosses 2M or at the moment of singularity formation.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Explain the horizon as the boundary of the past of scri+, which starts growing from the centre while the star is still larger than 2M, and use Fig. 25.11 to show this.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The opening says clocks 'at' r_S record no time and that signals from there are infinitely redshifted, without noting that no static observer can exist at r = 2M; later (margin note 12) the book warns that the static redshift formula does not apply to a falling emitter.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may picture a clock parked on the horizon that has stopped, which contradicts the chapter's later message that nothing local happens there.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Phrase it as a limit: static clocks placed ever closer to 2M tick ever more slowly relative to infinity, and hovering becomes impossible at 2M; a falling clock crosses normally.

tutor_notes: Open with a prediction question: 'An astronaut falls toward a black hole flashing a torch every second. What do she and a far-away friend each record?' Collect both answers before any formulas.

Order: (1) the two bad radii and the claim that one is fake; (2) light-cone slope and closing cones; (3) the sign test inside the horizon; (4) proper time versus coordinate time for the plunge; (5) tidal forces as the real-singularity detector; (6) photon delay and freezing; (7) the view from near the hole; (8) collapse and Penrose diagrams. Tortoise coordinates can be slotted after (6), where the logarithm has just appeared twice.

Check for understanding: ask the learner to set dt = dtheta = dphi = 0 in the metric at r = M and say whether a small step in r is timelike or spacelike, then ask what that implies for someone at r = M.

Check: 'If Schwarzschild coordinate time to reach r_S is infinite, why is it legitimate to say the astronaut crosses?' Look for the distinction between a coordinate label and a clock carried by the traveller.

Common question: 'Does the astronaut see the whole future history of the universe flash by as she crosses?' Answer no: that picture comes from confusing static and falling observers; a free faller receives only a finite amount of outside history before reaching r = 0.
Common question: 'Is the horizon a physical membrane?' Stress that locally it is unremarkable empty space; it is defined globally by which events can signal to infinity.
Common question: 'Why is the singularity drawn horizontal on the Penrose diagram?' Connect to the role swap: r is time inside, so r = 0 is a moment, like the Big Bang in Chapter 19.
Flag the misprint in eqn 25.10 when the learner reaches it, and have them verify the sign from dr/dtau = -(2M/r)^(1/2).
When using the half-sky result at r = 3M, say explicitly that it is for a hovering observer, and offer the falling-observer caveat to advanced learners.

Use real numbers to make tidal effects concrete: stellar-mass holes kill well outside r_S, supermassive ones allow a quiet crossing; horizon-to-singularity proper time is about 6.6 microseconds per solar mass for a fall from rest at infinity.
For learners who ask how to fix the coordinates, point to Exercise 25.1 (a one-line time shift gives Painleve-Gullstrand) before the heavier EF and Kruskal machinery of Chapters 26-27.
For novices, drop the tortoise coordinate details and keep only its moral: a clever label can straighten light rays but cannot by itself bring the horizon within reach.
